1 Introduction
Vision-language-action models in autonomous driving leverage
large vision-language models (VLMs) to integrate semantic rea-
soning and high-level scene understanding into driving decisions,
attracting significant interest for their potential in generalization
and scalability. Early work, such as LMDrive [35] demonstrated
the important role of vision-language models in following driving
instructions. Subsequent studies [22, 41, 63], show that reasoning
mechanisms based on language models can substantially improve
performance in complex driving scenarios.
Despite these promising results, existing VLA-based driving mod-
els often repeat similar mistakes in similar scenarios, lacking the
ability to directly associate the current situation with past failures.
Studies [2, 3] on human physiology and behavior have shown that
humans link ongoing situations with historical errors, predicting
the likelihood of failure in the current context and adjusting their
behavior accordingly. Motivated by this, we introduce an explicit
latent memory that records failure cases, enabling associative re-
trieval and error likelihood assessment at test time, allowing the
model to selectively adjust its planning based on prior failures.
In parallel, memory-augmented methods have shown strong
potential across agent systems, robotics, and sequence modeling.
Approaches such as MANTRA [31] and MemoNet [53] retrieve
prototypical trajectories for motion prediction, while agent systems
like JARVIS-1 [48] and MemGen [57] leverage episodic memory
for long-horizon decision-making. More recently, memory has also
been introduced into VLA-style embodied agents, such as Memo-
ryVLA [36] and EchoVLA [25], primarily to improve long-horizon
reasoning and task consistency.
Existing VLA-based methods in Embodied AI typically use in-
termediate vision-language features as retrieval keys for memory.
However, unlike robotic manipulation, autonomous driving plan-
ning relies more heavily on two types of intrinsic information:
(1) dynamic information (e.g., motion of surrounding agents),
and (2) scene structure information (e.g., road topology). Using
vision-language features directly as retrieval keys makes it dificult
to efectively capture these two critical aspects, leading to retrieved
cases that may difer significantly from the current scenario in
terms of dynamics and structure—diferences that are essential for
robust decision-making and failure recovery.
To address this, we propose DriveVLA-M0 1, a framework that
integrates failure-aware memory with test-time adaptation for VLA-
based driving. Our key insight is that efective memory augmenta-
tion for autonomous driving requires two properties: (1) structural
retrieval: retrieving cases based on scene-level similarity with re-
spect to dynamic and physical structure rather than vision-language
similarity; and (2) failure awareness: focusing on scenarios where
the base model underperforms.
Our approach consists of two stages. In the ofline stage (Mem-
ory Generation), we construct a latent memory pool by identifying
failure scenarios via oracle simulation metrics and storing their in-
termediate representations, including scene embeddings, trajectory
clusters, and expert signals. To enable efective retrieval, we train a
dedicated Retrieve Model that explicitly captures static road struc-
ture and dynamic agent interactions using a dual-branch design. In
the online stage (Inference with TTT), structurally similar cases are
retrieved from memory and used to adapt the action decoder via a
decoupled LoRA mechanism, enabling targeted, scenario-specific
adaptation with minimal overhead. The key advantage of DriveVLA-
M0 lies in the synergy between memory retrieval and test-time
adaptation: memory provides access to past and external failure
experiences, while TTT allows the VLA model to dynamically inte-
grate this knowledge into its driving policy. Together, they enable
the model to handle scenarios that were previously failure-prone
and improve robustness to distribution shifts without requiring
large-scale retraining.
Extensive experiments on NAVSIMv1 [8] and NAVSIMv2 [4]
demonstrate the efectiveness ofour approach. DriveVLA-M0 achieves
state-of-the-art performance across multiple metrics, reaching 94.1
PDMS on NAVSIMv1 and 47.0 EPDMS on NAVSIMv2, demonstrat-
ing superior results in safety-critical indicators such as collision
avoidance and drivable area compliance. Moreover, we show that
our framework scales naturally with external memory, enabling fur
ther gains through synthetic data augmentation without modifying
the base model. Our contributions are as follows:
• We propose a failure-aware memory augmentation frame-
work for VLA-based autonomous driving that explicitly tar-
gets poorly performing scenarios.
• We design a structurally grounded retrieval mechanism that
decouples static and dynamic scene features and integrate it
with a decoupled LoRA-based test-time training strategy for
eficient, targeted online adaptation.

2 Related Works
2.1 E2E Autonomous Driving and VLA Models
E2E autonomous driving learns a unified policy mapping raw sen-
sor inputs to planned trajectories [59]. TransFuser [6] introduces
transformer-based sensor fusion for multi-modal feature integra-
tion, and UniAD [14] jointly optimizes perception, prediction, and
planning through task-hierarchy design. DifusionDrive [24] mod-
els multimodal action distributions with a truncated difusion policy,
and GoalFlow, Mimir, and MeanFuser [46, 51, 52] reduce trajectory
divergence by conditioning flow matching on a scene-selected goal
point. The proposal-and-score paradigm [5, 11, 23] like iPad gen-
erates diverse trajectory candidates and selects among them via
multi-criteria scoring.
On the VLA side, DriveVLM [41] first applies large VLMs to pro-
vide semantic scene reasoning for driving. PlanAgent [58] studies
MLLM planning. OmniDrive [47] grounds an LLM agent in 3D driv-
ing tasks with counterfactual reasoning annotations. ORION [9]
couples a memory-augmented LLM with trajectory generation and
natural language explanations. OpenDriveVLA [62] aligns 2D and
3D visual tokens in a unified semantic space for planning. VLM-
Planner [39] adopts a fast-slow system design to integrate VLM
reasoning with eficient motion planning. AutoVLA [63] integrates
chain-of-thought reasoning and trajectory prediction in a single
autoregressive model with GRPO-based reinforcement fine-tuning.
AlphaDrive, DreamerAD, and ReCogDrive [16, 22, 54] combine re-
inforcement learning with VLM reasoning to handle safety-critical
and long-tail scenarios. Recent works such as SERA, ELF-VLA, Be-
yondDrive, and SoAD [10, 28, 45, 50] further exploit failure cases
or safety values, requiring extensive post-training. In contrast, our
method compresses failure contexts into a structured latent memory
for direct test-time adaptation without ofline retraining.

2.2 Memory-Augmented Methods
Memory augmentation enables models to store and reuse past ex-
perience at inference. In trajectory prediction, MANTRA [31] re-
trieves prototypical motion patterns from a memory bank, and
MemoNet [53] captures retrospective intentions from historical
agent trajectories for consistent multi-agent forecasting. In robot-
ics, JARVIS-1 [48] equips multimodal agents with episodic memory
for open-world task execution, MemGen [57] accumulates latent
memory without catastrophic forgetting, and STRAP [32] retrieves
sub-trajectories from a memory bank to augment policy learning.
Titans [1] proposes a neural memory module updated at inference,
and Memento [61] adapts LLM agents via external memory with-
out modifying model weights. Agent memory studies management,
retrieval, and utilization [30, 42, 43]. In driving, EvoVLA [27] builds
a self-evolving VLA through continuous experience accumulation,
MTRDrive [29] stores prototypical corner-case scenarios for rapid
retrieval, and MemoryVLA [36] introduces perceptual-cognitive
memory into VLA planning. However, these methods primarily
perform retrieval in the vision-language space, overlooking critical
structural properties of driving scenes such as road topology and
agent layouts, which can lead to retrieved cases that are semanti-
cally similar but structurally mismatched for safe decision-making.
2.3 Test-Time Training and Parameter-Eficient
Adaptation
Test-time training (TTT) adapts model parameters on each test
input to close the train-test distribution gap [38]. TENT [44] mini-
mizes prediction entropy on batch normalization statistics without
labeled data, and TTT++ [26] combines contrastive self-supervision
with feature alignment to handle natural distribution shifts. LoRA [12]
constrains weight updates to low-rank matrices for parameter-
eficient fine-tuning. LoRA-TTT [18] applies this to VLMs at test
time, and Test-Time Low Rank Adaptation [15] extends it with
confidence-based strategies for zero-shot generalization. STARAP [32]
shows that adapting with a small set of retrieved samples improves
out-of-distribution performance in robotic policy learning. In au
tonomous driving, Centaur [37] performs test-time training by
minimizing cluster entropy to reduce decision uncertainty. In con-
trast, we leverage memory to provide more explicit guidance signals.
Meanwhile, our method enables post-training-free scaling through
memory expansion.

2.2 Memory-Augmented Methods
Memory augmentation enables models to store and reuse past ex-
perience at inference. In trajectory prediction, MANTRA [31] re-
trieves prototypical motion patterns from a memory bank, and
MemoNet [53] captures retrospective intentions from historical
agent trajectories for consistent multi-agent forecasting. In robot-
ics, JARVIS-1 [48] equips multimodal agents with episodic memory
for open-world task execution, MemGen [57] accumulates latent
memory without catastrophic forgetting, and STRAP [32] retrieves
sub-trajectories from a memory bank to augment policy learning.
Titans [1] proposes a neural memory module updated at inference,
and Memento [61] adapts LLM agents via external memory with-
out modifying model weights. Agent memory studies management,
retrieval, and utilization [30, 42, 43]. In driving, EvoVLA [27] builds
a self-evolving VLA through continuous experience accumulation,
MTRDrive [29] stores prototypical corner-case scenarios for rapid
retrieval, and MemoryVLA [36] introduces perceptual-cognitive
memory into VLA planning. However, these methods primarily
perform retrieval in the vision-language space, overlooking critical
structural properties of driving scenes such as road topology and
agent layouts, which can lead to retrieved cases that are semanti-
cally similar but structurally mismatched for safe decision-making.
2.3 Test-Time Training and Parameter-Eficient
Adaptation
Test-time training (TTT) adapts model parameters on each test
input to close the train-test distribution gap [38]. TENT [44] mini-
mizes prediction entropy on batch normalization statistics without
labeled data, and TTT++ [26] combines contrastive self-supervision
with feature alignment to handle natural distribution shifts. LoRA [12]
constrains weight updates to low-rank matrices for parameter-
eficient fine-tuning. LoRA-TTT [18] applies this to VLMs at test
time, and Test-Time Low Rank Adaptation [15] extends it with
confidence-based strategies for zero-shot generalization. STARAP [32]
shows that adapting with a small set of retrieved samples improves
out-of-distribution performance in robotic policy learning. In au
tonomous driving, Centaur [37] performs test-time training by
minimizing cluster entropy to reduce decision uncertainty. In con-
trast, we leverage memory to provide more explicit guidance signals.
Meanwhile, our method enables post-training-free scaling through
memory expansion.

As illustrated in Figure 2, inspired by the mechanism by which

stage, the Retrieve Model retrieves structurally similar historical
scenarios from memory, and a Decoupled LoRA architecture is em-
ployed to perform test-time training of the planning head, thereby

4 Experiments
4.1 Benchmarks
We evaluate DriveVLA-M0 on two complementary benchmarks
spanning non-reactive open-loop simulation and reactive pseudo
closed-loop evaluation.
NAVSIMv1 [8]. NAVSIMv1 is a non-reactive, data-driven autonomous
driving benchmark built on sensor data from nuPlan [17] and
OpenScene [33]. It computes simulation-based metrics by unrolling
bird’s-eye-view (BEV) abstractions of scenes over a short simulation
horizon, during which the evaluated policy and the environment
do not interact. This decoupling enables open-loop metric compu-
tation while achieving better correlation with closed-loop evalu-
ations than traditional displacement errors. The primary metric
is the PDMS, which comprises five sub-scores. No-at-fault Colli-
sion (NC) penalizes collisions caused by the ego vehicle. Drivable
Area Compliance (DAC) measures whether the ego vehicle remains
within the drivable region. Time-to-Collision (TTC) assesses the
safety margin relative to surrounding agents. Comfort (C) penalizes
excessive jerk or acceleration. Ego Progress (EP) rewards forward
progress along the planned route.
NAVSIMv2 [4]. NAVSIM v2 extends v1 with a richer metric and
a pseudo closed-loop evaluation protocol. The metric is the Ex-
tended PDM Score (EPDMS), which adds four sub-scores to PDMS.
Lane Keeping (LK) checks whether the ego vehicle stays within its
current lane. Driving Direction Compliance (DDC) penalizes driv-
ing against the intended trafic direction. Trafic Light Compliance
(TLC) enforces adherence to trafic signal states. Extended Comfort
(EC) imposes stricter kinematic smoothness constraints. Evaluation
follows a two-stage pipeline: Stage 1 scores the initial planned tra-
jectory, and Stage 2 scores the planner on pre-computed follow-up
scenes that branch from the Stage 1 outcome, better approximating
long-horizon closed-loop behavior.

5 Conclusion
We present DriveVLA-M0, a failure-aware memory augmentation
framework that enhances VLA-based autonomous driving with
structured retrieval and test-time adaptation. Unlike prior methods
that rely on static model parameters and language-level embed-
dings, DriveVLA-M0 explicitly targets failure-prone scenarios and
retrieves structurally relevant cases based on road topology and
agent layout. A Decoupled LoRA TTT mechanism injects the re-
trieved knowledge into the Action Decoder in a scenario-specific
manner, activating only when necessary to minimize overhead.
Experiments on NAVSIMv1 and NAVSIMv2 demonstrate consistent
improvements over prior methods, with further gains achievable by
expanding the memory pool with synthetic data without retraining
the base model.

spans.content: Eficiency Analysis. Table 6 summarizes the inference-time
eficiency of DriveVLA-M0. All measurements are conducted on a
single NVIDIA H20 GPU with a latent memory containing 4,000
cases. The retrieval stage is highly eficient: querying the memory
takes only 15.19 ms. A single forward pass requires 30.79 ms. For
TTT, the backward pass with Decoupled LoRA takes 26.44 ms,
compared to 55.42 ms for full Action Decoder, demonstrating a
significant reduction in latency cost. Overall, these results show that
DriveVLA-M0 introduces only modest overhead during inference,
while enabling efective injection when TTT is triggered.
5 Conclusion
We present DriveVLA-M0, a failure-aware memory augmentation
framework that enhances VLA-based autonomous driving with
structured retrieval and test-time adaptation. Unlike prior methods
that rely on static model parameters and language-level embed-
dings, DriveVLA-M0 explicitly targets failure-prone scenarios and
retrieves structurally relevant cases based on road topology and
agent layout. A Decoupled LoRA TTT mechanism injects the re-
trieved knowledge into the Action Decoder in a scenario-specific
manner, activating only when necessary to minimize overhead.
Experiments on NAVSIMv1 and NAVSIMv2 demonstrate consistent
improvements over prior methods, with further gains achievable by
expanding the memory pool with synthetic data without retraining
the base model.
